title: Where to Play
hook: Four channels, five customer segments, three geographies. Everything accessible. Nothing chosen. The field that results from saying yes to every opportunity is not a strategy; it is a list of places where the organization happens to be present.
counterintuition: Narrowing your competitive field is not a retreat. It is the action that makes all the resources you are already spending start to compound. In a field you did not choose, those resources are spread too thin to create any advantage. In a field you chose, they point in the same direction.
tryThisNow: Name one customer segment, channel, or geography you are currently serving that you did not consciously choose: it just accumulated. Ask what you would have to stop doing in that segment to compete better where you actually want to win. Write the answer down before the next decision meeting.
keyTakeaway: Where to play is not a description of where you currently operate. It is a set of explicit decisions about which customers, channels, and geographies you will compete for, and which you will stop serving or not enter.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rosa's grooming studio served dogs of all sizes, cats, rabbits, and the occasional exotic bird. The studio was optimized for nothing in particular. The appointment schedule mixed an hour-long doodle groom with a fifteen-minute rabbit trim with a two-hour Persian cat appointment that required a second groomer.

When a colleague asked which animals Rosa was actually best at grooming, the answer was immediate: companion dogs under fifteen pounds, city apartments, owners who booked monthly. She was not best at the others. She was just willing.

Rosa was not losing the bird clients. She was choosing not to keep them. That is what a field choice is.

Within a quarter of naming her field, the studio schedule had space for six more monthly dog clients. She had stopped competing in the cat and rabbit market where a dedicated competitor had better tools and shorter appointment times. She was winning in the field she had chosen, not spreading across the field she had inherited.
breakdown.deepRead:
The where-to-play choice operates on multiple dimensions simultaneously. A business that asks where should we compete is actually asking several questions at once: which customers, in which geographic area, through which channel, in which category, and at which vertical level of the value chain. Answering one and leaving the others open is not a complete field choice.

Bounty did not win by being everywhere. It won by concentrating where the advantage was real and the value could be captured. The premium segment of the paper towel shelf was not the largest segment; the value tier was. But the value tier was also the most competitive and the segment where the margin was thinnest. Choosing the premium segment allowed Bounty to build the capability and pricing position that a value-tier choice would have required them to sacrifice. The field choice made the how-to-win choice possible.

Every field that is not chosen is inherited. Inherited fields are the customers who found you first, the channels where you happened to win an early relationship, the geographies where it was convenient to be. They are not bad starting points. They are not a strategy.

The two field traps are the same trap from opposite directions: serving too many segments in the belief that breadth is safety, or staying in the segment you inherited because changing it feels like loss. In either case, the investment you are making cannot compound, because it is pointed at too many places or the wrong one.
breakdown.fullRead:
Field choice is the most neglected of the five cascade choices, for a simple reason: most organizations already occupy a field when they begin thinking about strategy. The customers exist. The channels are live. The geography is defined by where the sales team already has relationships. Asking the organization to reconsider the field means implying that the existing customers, channels, and geographies are somehow wrong, which is uncomfortable to say to the people who built them.

An inherited field is not the same as a chosen one. An inherited field means you compete in the places where you happen to be. A chosen field means you compete in the places where you have decided you can win.

Bounty is the cleaner illustration. The premium segment for paper towels was not the largest segment on the shelf; the value tier was larger. But the value tier was also the most competitive and the segment where margin was thinnest. Choosing the premium segment allowed Bounty to build the capability and pricing position that a value-tier choice would have forced them to sacrifice. The segment choice created the arena in which the advantage logic could be built and maintained.

Now think about a field you occupy that you did not actively select. It might be a customer type you started serving because they asked and you said yes. It might be a channel where you have presence because a partnership made it convenient. It might be a geography where one early client gave you a foothold that never turned into a deliberate expansion.

Ask this question: if you could redesign where you compete from scratch, knowing what you know now, would you choose that same customer, channel, and geography? If the answer is anything other than clearly yes, the field is worth reconsidering. Not immediately and not painlessly, but as a strategic question, not a historical fact.

The dimensions of the field choice that matter: which customers (segment, size, behavior, economics); which channels (direct, indirect, digital, physical); which geographies (local, regional, national, international); which categories (the product or service type you are selling within); and which vertical level (manufacturer, distributor, retailer, service layer). Each dimension is its own explicit decision. Leaving any of them at the default is leaving a piece of the field unchosen.

A field chosen across all five dimensions gives the how-to-win choice a specific arena. A field that is a collection of inherited defaults is an arena with no defined boundaries, where the organization competes against everyone for everyone and wins on nothing in particular.

Name your field. All of it. Customers, channels, geographies, categories, vertical scope. Then ask which of those dimensions you actually chose.

examples.title: Sophie Names the Channel She Can Actually Win

planSpec.domain: a specialty food brand choosing between national grocery chain distribution and direct-to-consumer subscription
planSpec.audience: a founder who has been approached by a large grocery chain but whose margins depend on the direct channel
planSpec.stakes: accepting the grocery deal means competing in a channel where the brand has no advantage; refusing it means staying where the customer relationship is actually theirs
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sophie names the field she is choosing, not defaulting to the bigger channel

examples.scenario: 'We can get you into four hundred stores by Q3.' The buyer's offer sat in Sophie's inbox for three days. On one side of the spreadsheet: a grocery distribution deal, lower unit price, standardized packaging, a promotional budget the brand could not fund. On the other: eight hundred subscribers who paid full price every month and left product reviews without being asked. Sophie had built the subscriber list over two years by being available only through the brand's own site. The grocery deal would reach four hundred stores but require the brand to compete on a shelf where national players had lower costs and larger promotional budgets.
examples.whatToDo: Name the specific channel where the brand has a genuine advantage: the direct subscriber relationship and the full-price positioning it supports. Accepting the grocery deal means entering a channel where that advantage does not exist. Saying no to the grocery deal is not losing a channel; it is choosing the one where the brand can actually win.
examples.whyItMatters: A field choice is as much about which channels to leave as which to enter. A brand with a real advantage in one channel gives that advantage up the moment it enters a channel where the value equation is completely different.

examples.title: Andrew's Enrollment Data Shows Three Inherited Segments

planSpec.domain: an independent music school deciding which age groups and skill levels to serve
planSpec.audience: a school owner who offers lessons for beginners through advanced students across seven instruments
planSpec.stakes: the studio time, teacher credentials, and scheduling system are stretched across three segments, none of which the school owns
planSpec.requiredBeat: three years of enrollment data reveals a field that was never chosen and three competitors who have each taken one of the unchosen segments

examples.scenario: Three years of enrollment data told Andrew a story he had been avoiding. Adult beginners were canceling at twice the rate of other groups; he had been replacing them every quarter. Beginner children were the school's largest segment, but a competitor with a Suzuki-method program and a better parent waiting area had been winning that enrollment for two years. Advanced teens competed for spots in a university prep program that offered credentials the school could not match. By trying to serve all three segments, the school had become moderately adequate at each and genuinely strong at none.
examples.whatToDo: Look at which segment the current staff credentials, space configuration, and scheduling system actually support at a high level. Choose that segment explicitly and build the enrollment process, marketing, and program design around it. The other segments may continue on a limited basis, but they should not shape the infrastructure.
examples.whyItMatters: A music school that serves every age and skill level builds for no one in particular. The segment you choose should determine how the studio is scheduled, how teachers are hired, and what the student or parent experience is designed to achieve.

examples.title: Vincent's Referral Sheet Is Two Different Clinics

planSpec.domain: a physical therapy practice deciding between sports rehabilitation and general post-surgical recovery
planSpec.audience: a clinic director whose patient mix has drifted into both segments but whose staff skills and referral networks are concentrated in one
planSpec.stakes: two referral channels that require different billing systems, certifications, and scheduling cannot both be primary
planSpec.requiredBeat: the referral sheet makes visible what the practice's current infrastructure actually supports at a competitive level

examples.scenario: At 7:45, Vincent reviews the referral sheet before the clinic opens. Twelve incoming patients this week: six from an orthopedic surgeon group whose referrals require insurance pre-authorizations, hospital-system coordination, and a billing process that takes ninety days to clear; six from a sports medicine network whose athletes need weekend availability, performance-targeted protocols, and a direct-pay model that closes in forty-eight hours. The clinic's equipment and floor layout were built for post-surgical recovery. The sports medicine referrals were being seen in the same space, on the same schedule, by the same therapists. Both groups were getting adequate care. Neither group was getting the clinic that had been built specifically for them.
examples.whatToDo: Map the referral channels, billing systems, scheduling requirements, and staff certifications that each patient segment requires. Then name which segment the clinic's current infrastructure supports at a competitive level. The other segment is an inherited field, not a chosen one.
examples.whyItMatters: Two referral channels that require different clinic identities cannot both be primary. Choosing one means the other becomes secondary, which may mean redirecting those referrals or building the separate infrastructure to serve both at a genuinely competitive level.

examples.title: Giulia's Distribution Map Shows Presence Without a Field

planSpec.domain: a craft beverage brand deciding between on-premise bar and restaurant accounts and off-premise retail shelf distribution
planSpec.audience: a co-founder managing distribution relationships in both channels simultaneously with a sales team of two
planSpec.stakes: neither channel is generating reorders at the rate required to sustain the team's investment in it
planSpec.requiredBeat: an investor's question reveals that the brand occupies two channels without having actually won customers in either on the brand's own strengths

examples.scenario: Which of the two channels had the brand actually won a customer through from nothing, without a personal visit or a placement incentive? The investor's question caught Giulia mid-sentence. She had been describing the distribution plan: twenty-two on-premise restaurant and bar accounts, fourteen retail shelf slots across two regional chains. Every on-premise placement had required a personal visit, a tasting, and follow-up training with bar staff. Every retail placement was underperforming because the brand lacked the promotion budget to move product from shelf to basket. Both channels were live. Neither channel was winning on the brand's actual strengths. The investor was asking which channel the brand occupied versus which one the brand performed in.
examples.whatToDo: Track reorder rates and customer acquisition cost separately for each channel. The channel with the higher reorder rate and lower acquisition cost is the field the brand actually wins in. Name that as the primary field and build the sales team, inventory, and marketing around it.
examples.whyItMatters: Presence in two channels is not a field choice. A chosen field is where the brand's specific advantage: relationship depth, story, premium pricing, or occasion fit actually drives a repeat purchase without requiring a personal sales visit to make it happen.

examples.title: Tomasz Maps a Shifting Field Before He Picks One

planSpec.domain: a rural veterinary practice choosing between companion animal care and livestock medicine
planSpec.audience: a practice owner whose geography covers both farming communities and a growing suburban fringe
planSpec.stakes: the equipment, staff skills, and scheduling systems for each field are incompatible at the practice's current size
planSpec.requiredBeat: mapping the geographic trend reveals that the field is shifting and the practice has not yet chosen which direction to follow

examples.scenario: The scheduling board had three farm visits before 7 a.m. and a waiting room filling with companion animals at 8 a.m. Before: Tomasz ran a practice that said yes to every call. Farm visits, companion animals, the occasional wildlife rehabilitation referral. Each category required a different vehicle configuration, different medications, different hours, and different staff training. No category was being served at the level of a focused competitor. After: he mapped the geographic radius of each client type and found that the suburban fringe was growing at twelve percent per year while farm-visit demand had dropped twenty percent over the same period. The field was shifting beneath him. The practice had not yet chosen which direction to follow.
examples.whatToDo: Map the geographic trend for each patient segment over a three-year window. The segment growing faster in your geography is the field worth choosing explicitly. The field choice will then determine the equipment investment, the hiring plan, and the scheduling system.
examples.whyItMatters: A practice that serves two incompatible fields simultaneously cannot build the equipment, scheduling, or staff expertise that either field requires at a specialist level. The field choice is not about abandoning existing clients immediately; it is about naming which direction the infrastructure investment should point.

examples.title: Laura Discovers the Field She Already Won

planSpec.domain: an independent podcast choosing between a wide general-interest audience and a narrow professional listener segment
planSpec.audience: a host who has grown a mid-size audience without a clear positioning and is being pitched both advertiser sponsorships and professional association partnerships
planSpec.stakes: the general-interest advertisers require download scale the show does not have; professional association partnerships require content specificity the show has been avoiding
planSpec.requiredBeat: the listener survey reveals an inherited audience in a specific professional field the show never explicitly targeted

examples.scenario: You are looking at a listener survey where you expected to find a general audience and found a profession instead. Laura had built a mid-size podcast about decision-making and leadership for two years, designing every episode for a thoughtful and curious listener who could be anyone. The survey showed something different: sixty-seven percent of respondents described themselves as working in operations management or supply chain. They had found the show not because of the broad framing but despite it, through a niche forum recommendation. The last ten episodes had been planned for the general-curiosity audience Laura hoped to reach. The actual audience was already there, in a specific field Laura had never explicitly chosen.
examples.whatToDo: Review the listener, customer, or user data for the field you are actually winning in without trying to. Name that field explicitly: which specific person has already chosen you, in which specific context, and for which specific reason. Then ask whether your content, positioning, or product is designed for that person or for someone broader.
examples.whyItMatters: An inherited audience is a field you have accidentally won. The question is whether it is the field worth competing in deliberately, and whether the current positioning is compounding that advantage or obscuring it.

questions.prompt: What does the where-to-play choice determine in a strategy cascade?
choices: The specific customers, channels, geographies, and categories in which the organization will and will not compete.
The advantage logic the organization will use to beat competitors in its current market.
The investment budget allocated to each growth initiative for the planning cycle.
questions.explanation: Where to play is the multi-dimensional field choice that shapes all subsequent cascade choices. It is distinct from how to win (advantage logic) and from budget allocation (which is an execution decision, not a strategic one). Leaving any field dimension at the default means leaving part of the strategic choice unmade.

questions.prompt: A regional accounting firm has been serving individual tax clients, small business owners, and nonprofits for eight years, starting with whoever walked in. Which action would represent a genuine where-to-play choice?
choices: Continue serving all three client types but invest in a better scheduling system to handle volume more efficiently.
Name which client type the firm's staff expertise, software systems, and referral network actually support at a competitive level, and build the firm's identity around that segment.
Add a fourth service line to diversify revenue and reduce dependence on any one client type.
questions.explanation: Improving scheduling or adding services both leave the field undefined. Naming the client type to compete for explicitly forces decisions about the referral network, staff certifications, and pricing model. The other segments become secondary, not equal priorities, which is the difference between an inherited field and a chosen one.

questions.prompt: A craft beverage brand is present in both on-premise (restaurant and bar) accounts and off-premise (retail shelf) slots. Reorder rates are low in both channels. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
choices: The brand needs a larger sales team to cover both channels more aggressively.
The brand's product quality needs improvement before either channel can succeed.
The brand occupies two channels without the specific advantage, pricing, or capability that either requires: present in both but winning in neither.
questions.explanation: Low reorder rates in both channels is not a quality or staffing problem; it is a field problem. Each channel requires a different advantage logic: on-premise requires relationship depth and occasion fit; off-premise requires promotional budget and shelf placement. A brand without the capability for either channel's requirements will underperform in both.

questions.prompt: A specialty food brand sells through both direct-to-consumer subscription and national grocery distribution. Its margins are strong in the subscription channel and thin in grocery, where it cannot match the promotional budgets of national brands. What does this pattern reveal?
choices: The brand should focus on improving grocery margins by negotiating better slotting terms with the retailer.
The brand has a genuine advantage in the subscription channel and is competing in the grocery channel without one, which will gradually drain the margin the subscription channel generates.
The brand has successfully diversified its distribution risk by serving two channels simultaneously.
questions.explanation: The margin gap between channels reveals a field mismatch. The subscription channel supports the brand's pricing, relationship, and storytelling advantage; the grocery channel does not. Continuing in a channel without an advantage consumes resources that could be reinforcing the channel where the advantage actually exists.

questions.prompt: A music school serves beginner children, adult hobbyists, and advanced teens preparing for university auditions. The owner's staff is credentialed primarily for advanced technique instruction. Which action best represents a where-to-play choice?
choices: Name advanced teens as the primary segment and redesign the scheduling, marketing, and teaching around what that specific segment requires.
Invest in additional staff credentials to improve quality across all three segments equally.
Reduce program offerings across all three segments to improve overall margin per student.
questions.explanation: Investing equally in all three segments is the inherited-field pattern: no segment gets chosen. Reducing offerings is a cost move, not a strategic one. Naming advanced teens as the chosen segment and building the infrastructure around their requirements creates a field choice with downstream implications for the how-to-win choice and the capabilities needed to deliver it.

questions.prompt: A rural veterinary practice serves both companion animals in a growing suburban fringe and livestock on surrounding farms. The suburban companion-animal population is growing twelve percent per year while farm consolidation has reduced livestock-visit demand. What is the most useful strategic interpretation?
choices: The practice should invest in livestock-visit capacity to serve an underserved rural market before a suburban competitor expands.
The practice should hire a second veterinarian to handle both segments at a higher quality level.
The field is shifting: the practice has not yet chosen which direction to follow, and equipment investment, scheduling, and hiring decisions should wait until that choice is made.
questions.explanation: Adding capacity for the declining segment is investing in the wrong field. Adding staff without naming the field still leaves infrastructure pointing in two directions. The field shift makes the where-to-play choice urgent; the right next move is the choice itself, not the investment that would follow it.

questions.prompt: A podcast host discovers that two-thirds of her listeners work in one specific profession, despite the show being designed for a general-interest audience. What where-to-play action does this data support?
choices: Name the professional audience as the chosen field, redesign content and positioning around that specific listener, and pursue advertising and partnership deals calibrated to that field.
Continue designing for the general-interest audience to avoid limiting total potential listeners.
Add a separate profession-specific episode series while keeping the general-interest framing for existing episodes.
questions.explanation: The data reveals an inherited field: the show already wins in a specific professional segment without trying. Choosing that field explicitly allows content, positioning, and monetization to compound. Keeping the general framing while adding a separate series leaves the field unchosen and splits the audience without building advantage in either direction.

questions.prompt: Bounty concentrated on the premium segment of the paper towel market instead of competing across the full shelf. Which strategic logic does this illustrate?
choices: Premium segments are always more profitable than value segments in consumer goods markets.
Choosing one segment let Bounty build the pricing and positioning to win there; competing across the full shelf would have made that impossible to sustain.
Bounty's success was primarily driven by product quality, not by field choice.
questions.explanation: The Bounty case illustrates that field choice enables the how-to-win choice that follows it. Competing across the full shelf would have required Bounty to match the value tier's pricing while also maintaining a premium position, which is unsustainable. The segment choice created the arena in which the advantage logic could be built and maintained.

questions.prompt: A physical therapy clinic serves two referral channels: orthopedic surgeons (post-surgical patients, insurance billing, 90-day payment cycle) and a sports medicine network (athletic patients, direct pay, 48-hour payment cycle). Both are served at a moderate level. Which is the stronger strategic move: Option A, invest in a billing case manager to reduce the 90-day insurance cycle; or Option B, name one referral channel as the primary field and build scheduling, staff certifications, and infrastructure around it?
choices: Option A, because improving billing efficiency is measurable and reduces a concrete operational drag.
Both options equally, because they target different parts of the same underlying problem.
Option B: naming the field first is the strategic choice; billing efficiency is an operational fix within a field the clinic has not yet chosen to be in.
questions.explanation: Option A improves execution within an unchosen field. Option B makes the field choice that determines what operational improvements should follow. A billing improvement in the wrong field is still investment in the wrong field. The sequence matters: choose the field, then optimize the operations within it.

reviewCards.front: What are the five dimensions of a complete where-to-play choice?
reviewCards.back: Which customers (segment, size, behavior, economics); which channels (direct, indirect, digital, physical); which geographies (local, regional, national, international); which categories (product or service type); and which vertical level of the value chain. Each dimension requires an explicit decision.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between an inherited field and a chosen field?
reviewCards.back: An inherited field is where you currently operate by default: the customers who found you first, the channels that were convenient, the geographies where early relationships formed. A chosen field is where you have decided to compete because you can win there. Only the chosen field can be consistently won.

reviewCards.front: What did Bounty illustrate about where-to-play choices?
reviewCards.back: Bounty concentrated on the premium segment, bypassing the full shelf competition. This allowed Bounty to build the pricing and capability required to win in that specific arena, which would have been unsustainable while also competing in the value tier. The field choice made the how-to-win choice possible.

reviewCards.front: What does a brand lose by serving two incompatible channel types simultaneously?
reviewCards.back: Each channel requires different advantage logic, pricing, and capabilities. A brand present in both without the specific resources for either underperforms in both. Investment cannot compound toward advantage in either channel.

reviewCards.front: What question tests whether a field choice is explicit or still a default?
reviewCards.back: Ask: if you could redesign your competitive field from scratch, knowing what you know now, would you choose the same customers, channels, and geographies? If the answer is anything other than clearly yes, the field is worth reconsidering, not accepting as a fixed fact.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish a chosen field from an inherited one by tracing how each customer segment, channel, or geography was added. You practice naming the specific dimensions of the where-to-play choice (customers, channels, geography, category, vertical scope) and use the inherited-versus-chosen test to identify which dimensions are still at the default.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a new distribution or sales channel opportunity
ifThenPlans.plan: Before saying yes to a new channel, ask whether the brand or practice has the specific advantage required to win in that channel. A channel that requires capabilities you do not have is not a field extension; it is a second field that will drain resources from the first.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a product or service portfolio
ifThenPlans.plan: For each customer segment or category in the portfolio, trace when and how it was added. If it was added because the opportunity was convenient, not because it fit the chosen field, name it as an inherited segment and evaluate whether it belongs in the field choice going forward.

Before hiring for a new capability or building new infrastructure, confirm that the investment is required by the chosen field. An investment that serves an inherited segment may be spending resources in the wrong arena.

ifThenPlans.context: deciding whether to exit a segment or channel
ifThenPlans.plan: If exiting a segment or channel is under consideration, test whether that segment or channel was ever explicitly chosen. If it was inherited rather than chosen, exiting it is not a loss; it is completing the field choice that was never made.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one segment, channel, or geography you are currently serving that was never explicitly chosen. Write down when and how you started serving it. Ask whether, if you were designing the field from scratch today, you would choose it. If not, name one concrete action you could take to reduce your investment there.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, when a new opportunity, partnership, or customer request comes up, ask whether it fits the field you have chosen or whether it is a new field in disguise. Name it explicitly before deciding. Opportunities that require different customers, channels, or capabilities are not extensions of the current field; they are separate strategic choices that should be evaluated as such.

memorableLines.text: Rosa was not losing the bird clients. She was choosing not to keep them. That is what a field choice is.
memorableLines.why: The three-sentence sequence reframes what feels like a loss as an act of strategic clarity.

memorableLines.text: Bounty did not win by being everywhere. It won by concentrating where the advantage was real and the value could be captured.
memorableLines.why: The two-beat contrast names the mechanism that breadth prevents: concentration of resources where advantage is actually available.

memorableLines.text: An inherited field is not the same as a chosen one. An inherited field means you compete in the places where you happen to be. A chosen field means you compete in the places where you have decided you can win.
memorableLines.why: The three-sentence definition gives the reader language to apply the test immediately to their own field.
